# Academic Integrity Policy: AI Tool Use

## 1. POLICY FRAMEWORK

### 1.1 Permitted Uses

**Students may use AI tools to:**

- **Learning and understanding**
  - Explain concepts in different ways
  - Generate practice problems and quiz questions
  - Summarize readings or lecture notes
  - Translate academic materials for comprehension

- **Research and ideation**
  - Brainstorm essay topics and argument structures
  - Identify relevant sources and research directions
  - Organize literature review frameworks
  - Generate outlines before writing

- **Writing support**
  - Grammar and style checking (similar to Grammarly)
  - Paraphrasing suggestions for clarity
  - Feedback on argument coherence
  - Citation format assistance

- **Technical and analytical work**
  - Debugging code with explanation of errors
  - Checking mathematical calculations
  - Data visualization suggestions
  - Statistical method selection guidance

- **Accessibility support**
  - Text-to-speech for reading difficulties
  - Content simplification for ESL students
  - Note-taking assistance

**Requirement:** All AI use must be disclosed in a brief statement (50-100 words) describing which tools were used and for what purpose.

---

### 1.2 Restricted Uses

**Students may use AI tools with explicit permission and disclosure:**

- **Generating initial drafts** (with substantial revision required)
  - Only if assignment explicitly permits
  - Must rewrite/substantially revise (minimum 50% original revision)
  - Must demonstrate understanding through reflection

- **Code generation** (in programming courses)
  - Only with instructor approval
  - Must include comments explaining logic
  - Must be able to explain and modify code

- **Data analysis assistance**
  - May use AI to suggest analytical approaches
  - Must conduct analysis independently
  - Must interpret and validate results yourself

- **Experimental design**
  - AI can suggest methodologies
  - Student must justify choices and modifications

**Requirement:** Explicit written permission from lecturer before use; detailed disclosure statement required.

---

### 1.3 Prohibited Uses

**Students must NOT use AI tools to:**

- **Submit AI-generated work as their own**
  - Submitting essays, reports, or assignments primarily written by AI
  - Passing off AI outputs as original thinking

- **Bypass learning objectives**
  - Using AI to avoid engaging with course material
  - Submitting AI solutions to problems designed to teach specific skills

- **Academic dishonesty**
  - Hiding AI use (non-disclosure)
  - Using AI on closed-book exams or timed assessments (unless explicitly permitted)
  - Submitting identical or near-identical work to peers (collusion via shared prompts)

- **Misrepresent understanding**
  - Using AI to answer exam questions without learning the material
  - Submitting AI-generated responses to questions testing specific knowledge

- **Violate assignment specifications**
  - Using AI when explicitly prohibited
  - Using AI tools beyond scope of permission

- **Plagiarism and attribution failures**
  - Failing to cite AI-generated content used in work
  - Presenting AI suggestions as personal analysis without attribution

---

## 2. ENFORCEMENT STRATEGY FOR 200-STUDENT COURSE

### 2.1 Prevention-Based Approach (Primary)

**A. Clear Communication**
- Distribute policy in syllabus with examples (Week 1)
- Conduct 15-minute orientation session on policy
- Create one-page quick-reference guide with decision tree
- Hold office hours specifically for AI policy questions
- Post FAQs on learning management system (LMS)

**B. Assignment Design**
- **Scaffold assignments** to require intermediate steps:
  - Outline submission (Week 2)
  - Annotated bibliography (Week 4)
  - Draft with peer feedback (Week 6)
  - Final submission (Week 8)
  - *Rationale:* Difficult to fake understanding across multiple submissions

- **Include reflective components:**
  - "Explain one concept from this assignment in your own words"
  - "What was the most challenging part and how did you solve it?"
  - "How would you approach this differently next time?"

- **Vary assessment types:**
  - In-class writing (no AI access)
  - Oral presentations/vivas (tests understanding)
  - Problem-solving under time constraints
  - Group projects with individual accountability

- **Specify AI policy per assignment:**
  ```
  Assignment 3 (Essay): AI use PERMITTED for brainstorming 
  and editing only. Disclosure statement required. 
  Minimum 70% must be your original writing.
  
  Assignment 5 (Exam): AI use PROHIBITED.
  ```

---

### 2.2 Detection Methods (Secondary)

**A. Stylistic Analysis (Low-tech, scalable)**

For 200 students, focus on **high-risk assignments** (essays, reports):

- **Read strategically:**
  - Skim all submissions for obvious red flags
  - Deep-read only flagged submissions
  - Compare student's writing across assignments (consistency check)

- **Red flags to notice:**
  - Sudden improvement in writing quality mid-semester
  - Vocabulary/style inconsistent with previous work
  - Overly formal or generic language
  - Unusual phrasing for student's proficiency level
  - Perfect grammar in student with documented writing challenges

- **Verification questions:**
  - Ask student to explain a specific sentence or argument
  - Request they rewrite one paragraph in their own words
  - Ask them to identify the weakest part of their own work

**B. Plagiarism Detection Tools (Existing infrastructure)**

- Use institutional plagiarism software (Turnitin, etc.)
  - Many now flag AI-generated content
  - Set sensitivity appropriately (avoid false positives)
  - Use as screening tool, not definitive proof

- **Limitations to acknowledge:**
  - AI detection tools have 20-40% false positive/negative rates
  - Should never be sole evidence of violation

**C. Disclosure Statement Review**

- Require all students to submit disclosure statement
- Check for:
  - Vague or missing disclosures
  - Disclosures that don't match assignment content
  - Patterns of non-disclosure

---

### 2.3 Practical Enforcement Workflow

**For 200 students, use tiered approach:**

**Tier 1: Preventive (All students)**
- Clear policy communication
- Well-designed assignments
- Disclosure requirement
- *Time investment: 5-10 hours course prep*

**Tier 2: Screening (High-risk assignments)**
- Skim all submissions (5-10 minutes per assignment)
- Flag ~5-10% for closer review
- *Time investment: 15-20 hours per major assignment*

**Tier 3: Investigation (Flagged submissions)**
- Deep read + plagiarism check
- Verification conversation with student
- *Time investment: 30-60 minutes per case*

**Tier 4: Resolution (Confirmed violations)**
- Follow institutional procedures
- Document thoroughly
- *Time investment: 1-2 hours per case*

---

### 2.4 Student Conversation Protocol

**If violation suspected:**

**Step 1: Invitation (Non-accusatory)**
```
"I'd like to discuss your submission for Assignment 3. 
I noticed some elements I'd like to understand better. 
Can we meet Thursday at 2pm?"
```

**Step 2: Open-ended questions**
- "Walk me through your writing process for this assignment"
- "Explain this paragraph in your own words"
- "What does [specific term] mean in this context?"
- "How did you come up with this argument?"

**Step 3: Listen for understanding**
- Can student explain their own work?
- Do explanations match the writing?
- Is student defensive or confused?

**Step 4: Clarify if needed**
- "I'm concerned because [specific observation]. Can you help me understand?"
- "Did you use any AI tools on this assignment?"
- "Your disclosure statement says X, but the work shows Y. Can you explain?"

**Step 5: Document and escalate**
- Record conversation notes
- Follow institutional procedures
- Involve department chair/academic integrity office if violation confirmed

---

## 3. SAMPLE DISCLOSURE STATEMENT

**Required for all assignments using AI:**

```
AI DISCLOSURE STATEMENT

Assignment: [Name]
Date: [Date]

I used the following AI tools:
- ChatGPT (brainstorming essay structure)
- Grammarly (grammar checking)

Specific uses:
I used ChatGPT to generate 3 potential thesis statements, 
from which I selected and modified one. I used Grammarly 
to check grammar in my final draft.

Percentage of work AI-generated: ~5%
Percentage of work substantially revised by me: ~95%

I confirm that I have disclosed all AI use and that the 
majority of this work represents my own original thinking 
and writing.

Student signature: _________________ Date: _______
```

---

## 4. INSTITUTIONAL SUPPORT NEEDED

For this policy to work with 200 students:

- **LMS integration:** Automated disclosure statement template
- **Training:** Brief faculty workshop on AI detection and conversation skills
- **Resources:** Decision tree flowchart for common scenarios
- **Backup:** Clear escalation path to academic integrity office
- **Technology:** Access to plagiarism detection tools with AI flagging
- **Consistency:** Coordination with other instructors on enforcement

---

## 5. POLICY REVIEW & ITERATION

- **Semester 1:** Pilot with feedback survey
- **Semester 2:** Refine based on student/faculty feedback
- **Annual review:** Update as AI tools and detection methods evolve
- **Transparency:** Share enforcement data (anonymized) with students

---

## Key Principles

This policy balances:
- **Integrity** (preventing academic dishonesty)
- **Practicality** (enforceable with 200 students)
- **Fairness** (clear rules, consistent application)
- **Pedagogy** (assignments designed to prevent cheating)
- **Flexibility** (accounts for legitimate AI use)

The emphasis is on **prevention through design** rather than detection, which is more sustainable at scale.
